cycle/01-Cycle-Directions.html: This round put all three directions on real screens rather than settling them in conversation. Each gives something up in a different place: the calendar-only treatment is the most familiar and the best for exact dates, yet never shows the phase at a glance, while the ring-only treatment is the cleanest and most distinctive but drops the date grid entirely. Nothing was eliminated here — the purpose was to make that trade visible before committing to it.
cycle/02-Cycle-Chosen.html: Variant D was adopted: Variant C's glanceable ring stacked above Variant B's month calendar. The two questions a cycle screen has to answer — where am I in my cycle, and on which dates — proved equally non-negotiable, so neither single-element option survived on its own. Variant A's phase sentence was cut in the process; once the ring states the phase, repeating it in prose underneath adds nothing but noise.
cycle/03-Cycle-Color-Schemes.html: Six interface palettes were themed live onto the settled Variant D screen, recolouring ring, calendar, accents and text together. Blush Rose was chosen for its warm and gentle base. Nordic Dark and Editorial were rejected for reading as performance dashboards, Botanical Sage for feeling like generic wellness, and the incumbent Warm Clay for being too muted to carry four distinct phases.
cycle/04-Cycle-Color-Blush.html: Six variations within the warm-pink family, ranging from dusty through coral to rosé gold. No single option was locked: Dusty Rose read muted and sophisticated, Rose Mauve moody, and Rosé Gold luxe, each pulling the mood somewhere unintended. The family was clearly right and the exact temperature clearly was not, so the exploration widened into pastels rather than forcing a decision.
cycle/05-Cycle-Color-Flo.html: Six pastels drawn from Flo's own palette — lavender and periwinkle backgrounds, a signature coral-pink accent, and blush tints. Coral Pastel was kept and later locked in as the calendar palette. The lavender and periwinkle bases, including Flo Classic and Plum Rose, were rejected for reading as a direct impression of the competitor rather than an identity of Magdalene's own.
cycle/06-Cycle-Color-Peach.html: Purple was dropped entirely for this round in favour of peach and cream with soft coral and apricot accents. Blush Peach was adopted as the overall scheme. Apricot and Honey Cream skewed too sunny and cozy, while Petal Peach was so low in saturation that the four phases stopped separating; Blush Peach stayed warm while preserving enough contrast to keep them legible.
cycle/07-Cycle-Ring-Concepts.html: With the palette fixed, the only variable across these six was the circle itself. Day Dots was chosen: one dot per day, coloured by phase, with today enlarged. The gentler alternatives each bought calm at the cost of precision — Minimal Progress shows how far through the cycle you are but not which phase, and Single-Hue Bloom names the phase but loses the shape of the cycle. Day Dots reads softly while still accounting for every individual day.
cycle/08-Cycle-DayDots-Luteal.html: Only the luteal dots moved in this round, with period held at coral throughout. A distinctly pinker luteal was adopted, and the existing shade rejected for sitting almost on top of period — which made the ring hardest to read in exactly the stretch that matters most, the run-up to a period. The tuning was deliberately constrained to warm tones so that no purple re-entered the palette.
cycle/09-Cycle-DayDots-Period.html: With every other colour held fixed, five treatments competed to make the period dots unmistakable. Two were carried forward: Bigger + Bolder, and Soft Halo. The baseline and the single-variable treatments were rejected because size alone or shade alone still left period competing with three other phases for attention. The halo earned its place by creating prominence without recolouring anything, leaving the palette intact.
cycle/10-Cycle-DayDots-PeriodHalo.html: The two surviving treatments were merged rather than ranked, because each solved a different half of the problem: weight makes the dot register, while the halo draws the eye toward it. The combined dot — larger, deeper, and wrapped in a halo — was adopted, with the halo's exact character left open across three options: a standard ring, a tighter one, and a soft glow.
cycle/11-Cycle-ManageData.html: A single Manage data entry was placed beside the sync status, opening either Import, which pulls history from Flo, Clue or Apple Health, or manual entry of dates, flow and symptoms. Hand-backfilling was rejected as the primary path: cycle history is the one dataset a new user already holds somewhere else, and asking her to retype months of it would lose her before the product could say anything useful. This entry pattern went on to become the convention for every other module.
sleep/01-Sleep-Identity.html: The Sleep reading and its link chips were moved onto the module's own slate-blue accent. The app's default clay was rejected because it clashed with the blue Sleep icon sitting directly beside it. Giving each module a distinct accent also allows the domain to be recognised before its label is read.
sleep/02-Sleep-Chart.html: A duration chart was introduced, with Daily, Weekly and Monthly ranges, an average line that recomputes per range, and the 7h 20m baseline drawn across it. A bare nightly figure was rejected: six hours twelve only carries meaning when measured against her own norm, and the baseline turns the number into a judgment — short for her — without the product having to scold.
sleep/03-Sleep-Logging.html: Logging was consolidated into a single bottom sheet offering two paths, Connect app or Enter manually. Separate flows were rejected because both serve one intent, getting sleep data in, and splitting them would force a decision about mechanism before the user has even stated her goal.
sleep/04-Sleep-ManageData.html: The entry was renamed from Add manually to Manage data. The original label promised less than the sheet delivered, so anyone already wearing a tracker would reasonably skip a button that appeared to offer only typing. Naming the destination rather than one action inside it makes syncing discoverable.
sleep/05-Sleep-SingleEntry.html: The header + was removed, leaving the entry beside the sync status as the single way in. Two controls opening an identical sheet is a false choice, and the + carried the wrong promise — adding one night, rather than managing where the data comes from.
sleep/06-Sleep-EntryProminence.html: Having become the only entry point, the control was tested as a pill at three weights: outlined, soft-filled and solid. Leaving it as a quiet inline link was rejected, since it could no longer afford to look incidental — but neither should it outrank the sleep reading above it, so the weight was judged on screen rather than assumed.
sleep/07-Sleep-EntryFinal.html: The solid blue pill was adopted and the small manage icon dropped. The lighter weights were rejected for disappearing against the card background, and the icon for carrying no meaning that the word 'manage' was not already supplying.
sleep/08-Sleep-NeedCircadian.html: Sleep need and circadian rhythm were built as nested pages, with a chronotype quiz and two routes to recalibration. Requiring a seven-night calibration week as the only path was rejected: it is the accurate route, but a dead end for anyone wanting an answer today. Recalculating from nights already logged runs alongside it, with the window and night filters exposed so the estimate stays honest about what it rests on.
labs/01-Labs-Overview.html: This first full pass grouped markers by body system, each opening its own detail with a trend over time, normal against optimal range, cycle context, and a plain-language reading. A flat table of values was rejected outright: a lab report already is a table, and it is precisely what leaves people none the wiser. Grouping by system gives an untrained reader somewhere to start, and separating normal from optimal explains why an in-range number can still deserve attention.
labs/02-Labs-Actions.html: The marker-detail actions were rebuilt as self-describing cards — Start an iron experiment, and Add to clinician report — each opening a real destination rather than hinting at one. Bare buttons were rejected because both actions commit the user to something substantial: a ten-week protocol, or a document she will hand to a doctor. Neither consequence is guessable from a label alone.
labs/03-Labs-Experiment.html: Every marker now opens its own data-driven detail, but an experiment is offered only where there is something to act on. Attaching one to in-range markers was rejected: HbA1c at 5.2% has no intervention worth running, and offering one anyway would manufacture a problem and undercut the product's claim to provide information rather than alarm. In-range markers still route to the clinician report.
nutrition/01-Nutrition-Overview.html: Nutrition reuses the shape proved in Labs: the cycle phase leads, a glucose-steadiness hero follows, and nutrients are grouped by what to prioritise now, with each focus opening its own detail and iron linking straight to the low ferritin in Labs. Calorie-first tracking was rejected as the frame, being the one thing every competing app already counts and explaining nothing about a luteal-phase crash. Reusing the Labs structure also meant this module cost far less to learn than the first.
nutrition/02-Nutrition-ManageData.html: The Manage data sheet was split cleanly in two: Import became pure app syncing, while snap and scan moved into Log a meal, sitting above the manual fields beneath an 'or enter it yourself' divider. Filing capture under Import was rejected because import implies a connected source that keeps updating on its own, whereas a photo is a one-off entry the user makes herself.
nutrition/03-Nutrition-IronMessage.html: The Iron focus message was rewritten to state that she is getting about half her iron target and should prioritise the foods below. The previous line described a state and named a consequence but never said how far off she was or what to do first; the replacement quantifies the gap and points directly at the next action.
nutrition/04-Nutrition-FoodSources.html: The message promised foods that the screen never actually showed, so this round supplied them, tested three ways: chips under an 'Eat more of' label, a simple bulleted list, and cards carrying portions and iron content. The copy had been written ahead of the content. Cards proved the richest option because iron is only actionable with a portion attached — 'spinach' is not advice, whereas half a cup at 3.2 mg is.
The foods were being listed above a message instructing the reader to look below, so three fixes were compared. The integrated order was adopted, making the message the section header with the foods beneath it. Simply swapping 'below' for 'above' was rejected: it would make the sentence true while leaving the reading order backwards, when an instruction should arrive before the thing it refers to.
nutrition/06-Nutrition-IntegratedVariati: All three variants held the integrated order and varied only the visual treatment. Food cards with emoji were kept, since the emoji act as a fast visual key when scanning for something to actually eat. The highlighted-minimal list and the large-header grid were rejected, the latter for pushing the message so far from the foods that the two lost their connection.
nutrition/07-Nutrition-MessageStyleGoals: The emoji food cards were retained and extended with a per-food 'Add to goals' button. Checkbox items and tap-to-add icons were rejected because a checkbox implies 'did I eat this today', which is a logging gesture, whereas the intent here is forward-looking: committing to eat more of something, which belongs in goals rather than a diary.
nutrition/08-Nutrition-PrettierIconMessa: With structure and interaction settled, every variable except message styling was frozen to keep the comparison honest. Three treatments were compared — a soft box with a larger emoji, a two-line split with the action picked out in colour, and a highlighted key phrase — and none was locked.
nutrition/09-Nutrition-MoreMessageStyles: Six further message treatments were explored: a border accent, a circled icon, a gradient background, an oversized emoji, an underlined phrase, and a badge with divider. None was adopted. Every option decorated the sentence without making the size of the gap any clearer, which, three rounds in, pointed at the format being wrong rather than the styling.
nutrition/10-Nutrition-CreativeStyles.ht: This round broke the deadlock. The progress meter was adopted, drawing the fifty-percent shortfall as a bar rather than describing it in words. The alternatives — a friendly callout, a status card, split emphasis, a badge row and a playful frame — were rejected for restating 'half your target' in different clothes. Only the meter lets the gap be seen instantly, which is exactly what three rounds of sentences had failed to achieve.
nutrition/11-Nutrition-ProgressMeterVari: Six variations refined the meter itself. The version carrying a percentage label was chosen: the bar communicates the shape of the gap while the number pins it down. Dual numbers were rejected for making the reader perform the division herself, and the compact inline treatment for shrinking the bar until the gap stopped being legible.
nutrition/12-Nutrition-Final.html: The finalised module brings the chain to a close: the overview with cycle phase, glucose hero and grouped nutrients; both Manage data tabs; the Iron focus carrying the percentage-labelled progress meter and its Add to goals buttons; and a new goal sheet with a servings target and cycle timing. What began as an unclear iron message ends as a specific gap, named foods with portions, and a way to commit to one — the point at which the module was worth handing to hi-fi.
movement/01-Movement-Overview.html: Movement's job is to answer a single question each morning — how hard should I train today — read through the cycle. Three concepts were built out in full rather than argued on paper: a readiness ring, familiar and glanceable but at risk of feeling like just another wearable; a cycle phase-arc, the most differentiated view but the one needing the most teaching; and a guidance-first screen, the calmest and most on-voice. The choice is a judgment about feel, which only real screens can settle.
movement/02-Movement-Directions.html: The same content was given three different leads and compared side by side. The guidance-led reading was adopted as the default because it matches the product principle of saying what something means rather than how it works, while the fitness-rings dashboard was rejected for leading with numbers the user must interpret herself. The phase-arc remains swappable, being the one view no competitor offers.
movement/03-Movement-Activities.html: A new Activities section was tried in three layouts. The grid of tiles was adopted and carried directly into the next iteration. List rows were rejected as the densest but flattest option, collapsing every sport into an identical row, and sparkline cards for showing too few activities at once; the grid keeps all six types visible while giving each a recognisable identity.
movement/04-Movement-LogActivity.html: Building forward from the grid, this round defined how a workout gets logged: tap a tile or + Log an activity, choose the type, enter the details, and receive a confirmation tied to the cycle. Because logging is the action repeated most often, the entry form was deliberately shown two ways — structured fields, which are familiar and precise, against large steppers and effort chips, which are faster and more tactile.
movement/05-Movement-Activities-Complete: The Activities section was assembled into a single live screen: a this-week summary, the grid, per-activity detail on tap, and the full logging flow. Keeping logging in a separate section was rejected, since reviewing the week and adding to it happen in the same sitting, and splitting them would mean navigating away in the middle of the task.
movement/06-Movement-Activities-ManageDa: Adding data was brought onto the shared Manage data pattern, with a filled button beside the synced line opening a Connect app versus Log manually toggle. A Movement-specific pattern was rejected: the convention had already proved itself across Sleep, Labs and Nutrition, and consistency in the fifth module is worth more than a locally better alternative.
movement/07-Movement-Module-Full.html: The full module was wired together, with the overview linking into both the Activities section and the Fitness level profile, and Activities opening either per-activity detail or the Manage data sheet. Nothing was dropped here; the overview lead remains swappable to the phase-arc or rings direction, so the question left open back in iteration 2 can still be answered without rebuilding the module around it.
